vt.analysis:
Type: OpenClaw Skill
Name: memclaw
Version: 0.9.9

The memclaw skill bundle instructs the AI agent to replace OpenClaw's native memory system with an external tiered retrieval service. It requires the agent to install third-party binaries (@memclaw/bin-darwin-arm64 or @memclaw/bin-win-x64), solicit sensitive LLM and Embedding API keys from the user, and write them to local configuration files (config.toml). While these capabilities are aligned with the stated goal of advanced semantic memory, the instructions to bypass native features, the execution of external binaries, and the automated setup of background maintenance tasks (cron jobs) represent a high-risk profile without clear evidence of malicious intent.

llm.summary: The skill's instructions broadly match a memory plugin (installing an npm package, running local services, migrating local memory, and storing API keys), but several operational and provenance gaps — unverified npm binaries, automatic cron/service behavior, and file-read/write instructions — make the package suspicious until you verify the publisher and package contents.

dimensions.detail: The declared purpose (replace built-in semantic memory) aligns with the actions described: installing an OpenClaw plugin, starting Qdrant and a local cortex-mem-service, and doing migrations/searches. Minor inconsistencies: supported-platform table limits to macOS Apple Silicon and Windows x64 while some instructions include Linux paths; the skill text also references optional platform binary npm packages rather than embedding binaries in the registry metadata.
dimensions.label: Purpose & Capability
dimensions.name: purpose_capability

dimensions.detail: The SKILL.md explicitly instructs the agent to ask users for LLM and embedding API keys, write those secrets into plugin/config files, read local OpenClaw memory files (for migration), and rely on local services at localhost ports. Those behaviors are coherent with a memory-migration/install flow, but they entail reading/writing user files and handling secrets — actions that expand the agent's access surface and should be explicitly approved by the user.
dimensions.label: Instruction Scope
dimensions.name: instruction_scope

dimensions.detail: The skill is instruction-only in the registry, but it directs installing an npm package (@memclaw/memclaw) that will pull platform-specific binary npm packages. Installing npm binary packages that run local services (Qdrant, cortex-mem-service) is moderate-to-high risk if the package/publisher is untrusted. No homepage, repository, or publisher identity is provided in the registry metadata to validate the npm packages.
dimensions.label: Install Mechanism
dimensions.name: install_mechanism

dimensions.detail: The registry declares no required env or credentials, yet the instructions require you to supply LLM and embedding API keys and to store them in openclaw.json or config.toml. Requesting those keys is proportional for a memory system, but the skill will persist them to disk and the service may fall back to environment variables if config is missing — make sure you want those keys stored locally.
dimensions.label: Credentials
dimensions.name: environment_proportionality

dimensions.detail: The plugin claims to auto-start services and register a cron job (every 3 hours) to run maintenance commands. While the skill itself is not flagged always:true, installing the plugin creates long-lived background behavior (services and scheduled jobs) that persist beyond a single agent session and have file-system and scheduling effects. That persistence increases risk if the package origin isn't verified.
dimensions.label: Persistence & Privilege
dimensions.name: persistence_privilege

llm.guidance: This skill implements a local memory service that will install an npm plugin and platform binaries, ask you for LLM/embedding API keys, write config files to your home directories, read existing OpenClaw memory files, and register periodic maintenance tasks. Before installing: 1) Verify the npm package publisher and repository (source code, README, release history); if no repo/homepage is provided, treat the package as high risk. 2) Inspect the package contents (and any platform binary packages) in a safe environment or sandbox/VM before running. 3) Prefer supplying API keys via an approach you control (temporary keys, scoped keys, or environment variables) and back up openclaw.json and any memory files first. 4) Consider disabling autoStartServices/cron in the config initially and run services manually until you confirm behavior. 5) If you cannot validate the package origin, do not install it on production machines — test in an isolated VM. If you want, I can list specific checks to run (npm package inspection commands, files to audit inside the package, and the minimal config changes to minimize risk).
